Working with plans

From phoropter, commit 863bf8a, with uncommitted changes. It describes the tool, so it’s the same on every site phoropter generates.

A plan is a short markdown file that records what you were thinking before a piece of work: what you decided, what you turned down, and what you guessed, each with its reason and where the reason came from. The code shows what was done. The plan shows why, in a form you can argue with later.

This guide is the format, in the present tense. The plans that decided its rules are listed at the end, as history; nothing here needs them. Phoropter, the tool serving this page, reads plans written this way and links them to the code they're about.

An example

From mock-control, a plan about getting a library ready to publish:

## Decision: Selectors use the library's prefix, `mock-panel`
- where: `` scip-typescript npm @hypertheory-labs/mock-control . src/lib/panel/`mock-panel.ts`/MockPanel# ``
- quote: `selector: 'app-mock-panel',`

**Because (Jeff):** a rename is cheapest before the first publish. Breaking the class
apps is fine.

A heading says what kind of entry it is. The list says what code it's about, with a quote of the exact text as it was. The bold lead says where the reason came from. The quote no longer matches today, because this plan's own work renamed it, and phoropter shows both versions side by side.

1. Write the plan

Name it plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<name>.md. The date is the day you say "we're implementing this," and it's written only in the filename, so it can't disagree with a second copy. The name is any unique word that means nothing, so it can't turn into a category.

The frontmatter has base:, the commit you're deciding against. Then a # Title, and a short opening paragraph saying what the work is and why now, before any entries:

---
base: e92038c
---

# Get the library ready to publish

The class apps have used mock-control from inside the workspace. Before anyone installs
it from npm, its names and setup should be the ones we'd keep.

## Decision: …

Entries

Three kinds, each a ## heading:

  • ## Decision: <title>, then **Because (<source>):** and the reason in prose.
  • ## Decline: <title>, the same, for something you considered and didn't do. Only for alternatives someone actually raised. Never invent strawmen to look thorough.
  • ## Guess: <title>, then **Disproved if:** and what would show it wrong.

Reasons stay prose. A reason squeezed into a field gets shorter and worse.

Sources

Every reason says where it came from, in the parentheses: a person's name, measured, or Claude, not asked (or whichever agent). Combine them when that's the truth: Jeff and Claude, measured, then Claude, not asked. An agent told to do something won't ask why, so the record has to show when nobody said. A reason the agent guessed stays labeled that way until someone confirms it.

When a draft's open question went unanswered and its fallback became the decision, say so, under the drafter's own name: Claude, unanswered, so its fallback, or Copilot, unanswered, ….

Anchors

An entry can say what it's about, as a list under its heading:

  • - where: one of three things.
    • A file path, optionally narrowed with ›: a heading path in markdown (README.md › Setup › 1. Install), or a key path in JSON (package.json › version). It works in any language, with nothing installed.
    • A symbol, like a class or a method. Run phoropter symbols <file> and paste one of the lines it prints. You never choose an indexer or type a scheme: phoropter picks the indexer by the file's extension, and the symbol's first word records which one found it. phoropter indexers lists what this machine can index. A file with no named declarations, like a Program.cs of top-level statements, has no symbols: anchor its path, with a quote. How symbols are spelled, and how to write an indexer, is in indexers/README.md in phoropter's repository.
    • Another plan's entry: plans/<file>.md › <entry title>.
  • - quote: exact text from the file at the base, so a reader can tell which lines you meant. It's searched for only in the anchor's own file.
  • - where (new): something the work will create. No quote, since it doesn't exist yet.

Values go in code spans. When a value contains a backtick, use a double-backtick span: `a `b` c` breaks; `` a `b` c `` doesn't.

Anchor at the code as it is when you decide. The plan's own work will move it, and that isn't drift: drift is measured from where the work landed.

Keep a plan small enough for one person to review in one sitting.

2. Commit it before the work

That's how git shows the plan came first. From then on it's never edited. You don't revise what you believed; you write a new plan that links the old one.

3. Do the work, and depart from the plan when the code disagrees

Don't force a plan through code that doesn't share its understanding, and don't quietly do something else. Depart, and write it down in the as-built. Whether the departure was right is a later conversation.

4. Write the as-built

<plan>.as-built.md, beside the plan. Its frontmatter has head:, the commit where the work landed. Its anchors point at that commit, because they're about code the work made.

Three kinds of entry:

  • ## Changed: <title>: the work departed from the plan. **Because (<source>):**
  • ## Chose: <title>: the plan left something open, and you decided it. **Because (<source>):**
  • ## Answered: <the guess's own title>: one of the plan's guesses, answered against its Disproved if. **Answer (<source>):**, then one of held, disproved, partly disproved, or not tested, then how much evidence that rests on.

Keep departures and choices apart. A reviewer wants the departures first, and Chose: is the comfortable label.

Anything else worth knowing, like a finding that isn't an answer to a guess, goes in the as-built's opening prose, not in an entry.

An as-built can say nothing changed. Nothing requires one, and nothing flags a missing one.

5. It freezes

An as-built is frozen once someone else could have read it, because from then on someone may have anchored to it, and it mustn't change underneath them. Before that, fix it freely. When that is depends on how your team shares work: a push, a pull request, a merge. If you're unsure, treat it as frozen once it's merged into your main line. Anything learned after that belongs in a new plan or a revisit. Phoropter can't tell when this happened and doesn't check; it's advice with a reason, not a rule it enforces.

6. When an earlier plan's ground is wrong, revisit it

If the work runs into something an earlier plan decided or assumed, don't decide it inside the current plan; that re-decides the old plan in the wrong frame. Stop, and say so in the current as-built: ## Changed: "stopped here; revisiting …". Then write a revisit: a new plan with revisits: plans/<file>.md in its frontmatter, naming exactly one plan. It asks the question in that plan's frame, and every reason says what moved: the world, the code, or your understanding. The outcome can be "it still holds." Revisiting your own plan is the same move.

Sometimes the earlier plan never wrote down what it assumed. Then the revisit anchors where the assumption shows, in the code or the docs, and says it wasn't in the plan. That records a gap in the old plan, which is worth knowing too.

To answer a guess from an earlier plan, restate it as a ## Guess: in your plan, anchored at the original, and answer it in your as-built.

Drafts (optional)

Most plans are never drafts: they go straight to plans/. A draft is for when the agent's confidence or the shared understanding is thin, or when the pair has agreed, for a session, that the person sees every plan first, not to judge it but to follow it. Who decides that is the pair's to work out. It's never an approval gate: a draft serves the agent's confidence and the person's understanding, not permission.

Work in progress lives in drafts/, at the repository's root, and plans/ holds testimony and nothing else. A repository has at most one draft, drafts/plan.draft.md. One fixed name means anyone can see whether a plan is being drafted, and drafts can't pile up into a backlog. Each branch or worktree has its own working tree, so parallel work isn't blocked. A draft that wants to be two plans gets smaller; the rest waits for the next one. Ignoring drafts/ in git is a suggestion: on a branch, committing it lets a mentor or senior read a draft before the code exists. On main, what lands is plans.

Annotations go in drafts/plan.draft.notes.md beside it, in the annotating agreement's format. An open question is one of that agreement's prompts, at any heading level below the entry it belongs to, with what happens if nobody answers:

### Question: Should phoropter also look anywhere else for a draft?
**If unanswered:** no. One name, and nothing else to configure.

Select lists its options as the first bulleted list; Affirm is yes or no. A draft can have no questions at all: "look, then tell me to go." The person answers in notes beside the draft, or in conversation. Don't turn a draft's prompts into a form: they're there to be thought about at the person's pace, in context.

The notes quote the draft's lines, so while a notes file exists, the draft doesn't change. To answer the notes before converting, rewrite the draft taking in every note, then delete the notes file: all of them or none. A reply that isn't a rewrite (an answer, a confirmation) goes in conversation, and the draft stays as it is.

When the pair is confident, the draft converts, whether or not every prompt is answered, since silence means proceed. Converting writes plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<name>.md (the date is today, the day you say "we're implementing this"), folds each answer into its entry's reason, labels a fallback that became the decision (<the drafter>, unanswered, so its fallback), drops the prompts, and deletes the draft and its notes. The notes aren't kept: they're mostly the questions that lined up someone's understanding, and what mattered from them is in the reasons now. An answer that turns down a question's premise, or creates work the draft didn't have, becomes an entry of its own, usually a Decision, not a clause in another entry's reason.

Phoropter's dev server shows the draft at draft/, re-read on every request, with its anchors resolved, its prompts and their fallbacks and answers, and each annotation after the entry it quotes. It says it's the working tree, not a commit. A built site never contains a draft.

Notes on a landed plan

A landed plan is never edited, but it can take notes: a person saying the plan matters to something now. For plans/2026-10-31-ramie.md, the notes are drafts/2026-10-31-ramie.notes.md, in the same format as a draft's, and their annotates: line names the plan. A note quotes an entry's heading line to be about that entry, or has no quote to be about the whole plan. The agreement puts notes beside their file. These live in drafts/ instead, so that plans/ holds only testimony. A landed plan never changes, so the quotes can't come loose.

A note may say the plan's ground has moved, or "weigh this in what we're deciding now", or just say something. Answer it in kind:

  • A revisit, when the ground has moved: a draft whose revisits: names the plan, and whose opening says what moved, citing the notes. Converting it deletes the notes it answered.
  • A citation, when the plan bears on the work at hand: the current draft anchors the entry the note is about, and its reason weighs it.
  • A note in reply, when the agent thinks the plan holds, or there's nothing to do.

Notes stay until the person who wrote them is satisfied, and nobody holds a veto: the person can always ask for a revisit.

On a branch, committed notes are how a teammate says "look at my branch, here's what I'm thinking about this old plan." Some teams keep a long-lived branch for this kind of work. That's a way of working, not a rule. Phoropter's dev server shows a plan's notes on its page, after the entries they quote, and counts them on the home page. A built site never shows them.

Older plans

Plans are read as written. Plans from before a rule here existed may use earlier forms, like an as-built that uses Changed: for everything, or a cart: line. Phoropter shows them as they are and doesn't rewrite or flag them.

Squash merges and rebases

Plans record commits: base: and head:. A squash merge or a rebase replaces the work's commits with new ones, and the as-built was written before that happened, so its head: names a commit that isn't on your main line. Once the branch is deleted, that commit may be gone. Phoropter doesn't reconcile this today: when head: isn't a commit it can find, it shows the text as written, and the as-built's anchors are shown only at the generated commit. Plans read best on a history of meaningful commits that are merged, not squashed. Not yet seen in a real repository.

Reading the site

Every page says which repository and commit it was generated from. Served by phoropter, the site follows HEAD as commits land. The home page lists plans oldest first and the places they anchor; each place lists the plans that touch it, newest first. The profile defines every link relation and microdata property, so an agent can read the same pages a person does.

Where these rules came from

Each rule here was decided in a plan, and those plans hold the reasons in full. They're history: most are in private repositories, their names mean nothing by design, and nothing above needs them. They're listed for anyone who has access and wants to know why.

  • The format, its file names, entries, sources and anchors; committing the plan first; departing from it; keeping plans small enough to review in one sitting, which is still a guess: aide's lanyard, the first plan.
  • As-builts and their three kinds of entry: aide's grommet. Reading the verdict as structure, and keeping findings in the opening prose: phoropter's burlap.
  • When an as-built freezes: aide's awl said "committed"; phoropter's twill made it "once someone else could have read it".
  • The double-backtick rule: phoropter's, after awl wrote one wrong.
  • Revisits: aide's bodkin. Burlap is one, reversing quince. An assumption the old plan never wrote down: mock-control's tallow. Answering an earlier plan's guess: mock-control's vellum.
  • Labeling an unanswered fallback: phoropter's sorrel and marl.
  • Drafts: phoropter's loden. drafts/: tarlatan. Notes on landed plans: tarlatan and organza.
  • Squash merges and rebases: phoropter's twill.
  • Answers that become their own decision, and these citations moving here: phoropter's poplin, from the first repository outside phoropter to use it.
